chapter: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
title: The ice cream cone, and being treated warmly in Southern white restaurants
summary: He recalls his father steering him past a whites-only ice cream shop; on southern tours of the thirties he sometimes found white restaurants unexpectedly friendly.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you -- after you had left the South and come north, and then when you went back with bands, with any group such as Claude's, did you ever have any real trouble? In the South.

Uh, I'm trying to think. Yeah, I have -- I'm trying to pin it down, because you would run into -- I'm glad you asked me that, because being born in the South I knew what to expect, and I knew what one could do, should do, or shouldn't do.

See, because well, when I was born, from a little baby up, I wondered about these things, and -- you know, I saw, and I learned. It's one thing that puzzles me, and I've never been able to shake it. My father had me out one day, and he was going to buy me an ice cream cone, and he said we're going down -- now come on. I said well why can't we stop here? At this little ice cream -- he said no, we're going down to the other. I said what? They sell ice cream here. And he didn't want to tell me, explain to me that we could not go in there and buy it. He was going to take me where he would have

less trouble. I mean I realized that later, many years later. But I couldn't understand, why did he go -- what do you want to go way the hell, way down there, around the -- you know, when we could get it here. You know?

Okay, as I told you, I learned. Now, in the -- after I joined these bands, and we went down south, all the way down to the bottom, and back here, then we got up, you know, not exactly a chip on the shoulder, because you don't do that, I mean you say well, you walk into a place with your head down, because you expect -- you're expecting -- generally expected that there was going -- something is going to happen to you.

So anyway, and you go in, and you don't get it. And you're treated damn nice, and with a smile, well when are you fellows coming back through here? Be sure and stop now. We will be looking for you, and stop in and eat with us, and just different restaurants. We said well thank you, we will. You know. Well that makes your food --

Yes! And they -- and it makes your food digest better, and you say well, that's -- you know. Instead of the guys looking at you, say don't come in here, that way, what you come in here for? What do you want? You know, and that -- well, if they're going to give you the meal you still don't -- you don't enjoy it.

So that happened a lot of times, and we came in, hi fellows, hey, they remembered two or three names. Come on over! Sit down! And the waitresses would be running, grabbing this, and grabbing that, and the managers, and the bosses and what not, everybody, you know. Sit down, be there. Be happy. what did you see? What do you like? Is the meat this and that? You know?
And you say well confound, these people have changed, or something, or they think we're human after all. Anyway, it becomes delightful.
Was this in the thirties that you're talking about, about the time when you went down with Claude?
It was -- even that far back.
Oh sure, because the thirties, yes. Even the forties, later than that, the fifties even, are you kidding? Sure.
No, but I mean that you were greeted pleasantly in white restaurants. (inaudible).
